claims.text: The nanoparticles are equiatomic AuCoCuNiPt particles smaller than 10 nm.
The initial nanoparticles have an FCC multi-twinned or icosahedral structure.
The nanoparticles were synthesized by pulsed laser deposition at 873 K on a silicon nitride membrane.
Heating above approximately 673 K activates non-sluggish atomic diffusion in these nanoparticles.
Surface-energy minimization drives the thermally activated atomic diffusion.
Au and Cu have sufficiently low surface energies to segregate preferentially to the nanoparticle surface.
Increasing temperature increases the mobility of surface atoms.
Shape changes from elliptical toward spherical enhance local atomic diffusion.
Au/Cu surface segregation and enhanced diffusion lead to evaporation of Au and Cu.
Au/Cu segregation and evaporation destabilize the initial solid-solution structure.
Particles in the 2–4 nm size range will progressively disappear during heating.
The nanoparticle size distribution will widen as temperature increases.
The average nanoparticle size will decrease because of Au/Cu evaporation.
Above approximately 673 K, the particles will transition from icosahedral or elliptical morphologies toward more spherical morphologies.
Entropy stabilization and sluggish diffusion theoretically favor retention of the initial particle size, shape, and solid-solution structure.
The predicted instability applies under vacuum during controlled heating to 973 K, particularly at or above approximately 673 K.
The onset temperature and extent of segregation and evaporation depend on initial particle size, shape, and synthesis details.
The experiment will heat the nanoparticles from 298 K to 973 K at 1 K/s under vacuum and examine them at 473, 673, 773, 873, and 973 K.
STEM-EDS and molecular-dynamics simulations can measure surface enrichment, morphology, and atomic diffusivity during the heating sequence.
Failure to observe increased Au/Cu surface concentration, shape transformation, or appreciable size reduction above approximately 673 K would falsify the hypothesis.
